tags.name: banking.v1.AllocationsService
tags.description:
AllocationsService — the registry of investable products (the Allocation primitive).

 An allocation is the control-plane record that makes a service id investable. It is
 the ONLY way one comes into existence: `FundsService.Subscribe` refuses a service
 with no registered, open allocation, so a user can never mint a fund by typing an
 unknown slug. Money never flows through this service — amounts, units and NAV stay
 on FundsService/BalanceService; here live identity, presentation, lifecycle and
 access only.

 Lifecycle: `draft` (registered, not yet accepting money) → `open` (subscribe +
 redeem) → `closed` (redeem only, so a closed product never traps an investor).
 `closed` → `open` re-opens. Registration and every transition require
 `AllocationManage` (Admin/Owner) — the same trust seam as posting a valuation.

 Access is a second axis, orthogonal to the lifecycle. `state` says whether the
 product takes money at all; `access` says WHO may see it and who may put money in.
 Every allocation carries a default level — `hidden` | `view` | `invest` — and an
 operator may raise one investor above it with a per-user grant (`view` | `invest`).
 The level a caller effectively holds is the higher of the two. A registration lands
 on `view`: visible, but locked until an operator opens it or grants the investor.

 Reads are open to any authenticated user, filtered by that effective level:
 `ListAllocations` returns only `open` allocations the caller may at least view, and
 `GetAllocation` answers NOT_FOUND for one the caller may not — unless the caller
 holds `AllocationManage`, who sees everything in every state. `Subscribe` refuses
 (FAILED_PRECONDITION) unless the caller's effective level is `invest`; `Redeem` is
 never gated on access, so locking a product cannot trap an investor. See
 docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

 The one place this service touches supply is `IssueUnits`: an operator minting units
 IN KIND — to an investor — with no cash behind them, for a product registered against
 an asset that already exists and already has owners. It lives here rather than on
 FundsService because it is a registry decision about who holds what, made by the same
 `AllocationManage` holder who sizes the product, not an investor dealing at NAV. The
 holder is always a PERSON: the company is not a holder (#245 — every unit of value is
 somebody's), and a reserved allocation (`fee`) comes to hold a product's fee class
 only through the fee accrual, never through this surface. `RetireUnits` is the mirror
 of `IssueUnits`: a holder's units burnt with no cash leg, supply shrinking by exactly
 that. It is Read-First on what the holder has AVAILABLE (units resting on the book or
 reserved by a redemption cannot be retired), and the burn shows in `ListUnitHolders`
 like any other supply change.

 Backing is the third axis. Units minted in kind have no cash in the fund's claim
 behind them, so `Redeem` — which pays cash out of that claim — is refused on a product
 whose `backing` is `in_kind` (FAILED_PRECONDITION); holders exit through the book. The
 first `IssueUnits` flips a product from `cash` to `in_kind` on its own; an operator
 flips it back with `SetAllocationBacking` once the fund does hold cash for the units.

tags.name: banking.v1.AuthService
tags.description:
AuthService — the money plane's token issuance and authorization surface.

 This is the MONEY plane: it does NOT do third-party (Google) OAuth — identity and
 sign-in live wholly in the concierge plane. Users are mirrored here by the one-way
 cross-plane bridge (concierge `CREATED` → a local row keyed by `auth_subject`).
 This service only issues/rotates the hub's OWN first-party asymmetric JWTs
 (EdDSA/Ed25519, `aud=banking-core`) for those already-identified users, and
 publishes verification keys. Services do NOT call this per request to authorize:
 they verify access tokens locally against the cached JWKS via the shared
 `evbanking_auth` flow (no round trip, no per-service token storage). They DO call
 `Jwks` periodically to refresh that cache, since the hub speaks only gRPC (no HTTP
 `.well-known` endpoint).

 `IssueUserToken` is the concierge→banking token-exchange seam: after the cabinet
 BFF authenticates a user against concierge, it calls this server-to-server (with the
 shared bridge issuance token, NOT a user token) to mint the money-plane pair for that
 user. Banking trusts its OWN service credential, never concierge's issuer — so a
 leaked concierge token can't move money. See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

tags.name: banking.v1.FundsService
tags.description:
FundsService — a user's investment in funds via the service currency (units/shares).

 Subscribing buys units at the current NAV; a holding's value is units × NAV, so
 profit comes from NAV rising, not from extra units. Redeeming is accept-and-queue:
 units are reserved immediately and the cash is priced + paid at settle (settle-time
 NAV). Every amount/unit/price is a decimal STRING (proto3 has no u128; a string is
 lossless and matches proto-loader's `longs: String`). Self-service RPCs act on the
 caller's own access-token `sub`. See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

tags.name: banking.v1.BalanceService
tags.description:
BalanceService — the bank's treasury and the platform's own allocations (operator
 surface).

 Reads authoritative balances from the TigerBeetle ledger; metadata and events from
 Postgres. Every amount is a decimal USDT STRING (proto3 has no u128; a string is
 lossless and matches proto-loader's `longs: String`). All RPCs are admin-gated
 (allowlist) at the boundary. See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

 The allocations hold no company money (#245): what they earn is the `fee` allocation's
 and what they were seeded with is the `fund` allocation's, and both are held by PEOPLE
 through units — so the treasury lists every allocation with its holders, and nothing
 here pays "the fund" out. Cash leaves a reserved allocation by a holder's redemption
 or by a payment the owners' consilium approved (`PaymentsService`). banking's own money
 is its treasury, `scope_account:main:treasury` (D17): the withdrawal fees it keeps, which
 nothing pays out until concierge's scope approvals decide its spending
 (`bank:treasury_surplus`, D24).

tags.name: banking.v1.BookService
tags.description:
BookService — the secondary market in an allocation's units: holders trading with
 each other on a central limit order book, price-time priority, in the shape of a spot
 exchange.

 It sits BESIDE the fund's own dealing, never instead of it. FundsService.Subscribe and
 Redeem are dealings with the fund at NAV; the book is holders dealing with holders at
 whatever they agree. NAV stays the accounting price — a position, its P&L and the fee
 high-water mark are measured at it — and the book's last trade is a second, market
 quote shown next to it (`BookSnapshot.nav` carries the mark so a ticker can show both).

 Money never leaves the ledger's custody: a resting order is an ESCROW inside it. A sell
 moves its units from the holder's `shares` account into a per-user book escrow, a buy
 moves its worst-case cash — size × price plus the taker fee it might owe — from the
 user's claim into a per-user cash escrow. A fill is ONE linked TigerBeetle batch (units
 to the buyer, cash to the seller, the taker's fee to the fund): delivery versus payment
 or nothing. Whatever the escrow still holds when an order ends is handed back, so a buy
 that filled below its limit, an IOC remainder and a cancel all release the difference.
 The hub records the order and its fills first (Postgres, under one lock per book) and
 the ledger moves follow through the same outbox relay as every other money event, so
 the balances a client reads lag a placement by the relay's latency, exactly as after a
 Subscribe.

 Who may trade: any signed-in investor whose effective access on the allocation is
 `invest` — the same gate as Subscribe, EXCEPT that the allocation's `state` does not
 apply (a `closed` product's holders may still trade among themselves; only `book_open`
 on the policy, `hidden` and `view` refuse). Placing is also refused while the money
 plane is in read-only mode or the caller is frozen; cancelling never is, so a frozen
 user can still unwind. The policy (fees, tick, lot, slippage, whether the book is open
 at all) is set by an `AllocationManage` holder; a product with no policy row has a
 closed book.

 Every amount, size and price is a decimal STRING (proto3 has no u128; a string is
 lossless and matches proto-loader's `longs: String`). Enumerations are strings too,
 pinned in `evbanking_contracts::book`. See piggybank/core/PATTERNS.md.

tags.name: banking.v1.ConsiliumService
tags.description:
ConsiliumService — multi-owner authorization over the platform's own money and its
 price: a payment out of a service claim (opened inside `PaymentsService.OpenPayment`),
 a NAV mark past the move guard, a change of fee terms beyond the house envelope, a new
 holder of a reserved allocation (`OpenHolderGrant`), and a seed of the platform's
 capital (`BalanceService.SeedCapital`). One owner opens a request; strictly more than
 half of ALL owners must each confirm it from their mailbox before anything happens.

 The kinds, as the `Consilium` message tells them apart (exactly one terms sibling is
 set): `payment`, `valuation_override`, `fee_policy`, `holder_grant`, `seed_capital`.
 (`revenue_payout` was retired by #245 and left the contract with C-9; field 3 of
 `Consilium` and `ConsiliumInvitation` is reserved for it.)

 WHY THE MONEY PLANE OWNS THIS. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md rejects letting a
 concierge-signed artifact authorize money movement, and a consilium verdict is
 exactly such an artifact. So the tally is computed, stored and verified here, against
 the owner roster this plane already mirrors (`0016_user_role.sql`). Concierge is used
 only to DELIVER the mail, over a typed payload it renders itself.

 QUORUM. `threshold = floor(N / 2) + 1` where N is the owner count at open. The
 initiator is in the denominator but gets NO vote and is never minted a token — so
 opening a request can never lower the bar the initiator has to clear. N < 3 makes
 the threshold unreachable and is refused at open rather than parked forever.

 IMMUTABILITY. There is no edit RPC. `payload_hash` binds every approval to the exact
 terms shown in the mail; changing anything means cancel and reopen, and votes are not
 carried over. See docs/CONSILIUM.md for the full policy and threat model.

tags.name: banking.v1.ConsiliumApprovalService
tags.description:
ConsiliumApprovalService — the surface an emailed owner reaches. Mounted OUTSIDE the
 user-auth layer, exactly as AuthService is: the emailed token IS the credential, and
 the owner clicking it may not be signed in.

 The GET is strictly read-only because mail scanners (Gmail, Outlook SafeLinks,
 corporate gateways) issue automatic requests for every URL in a message. The vote is
 a separate call carrying the secret code from the same mail — that is what turns a
 scanned link into a deliberate human act.

tags.name: banking.v1.FeesService
tags.description:
FeesService — a fund's management and performance fee ("2 and 20").

 Two charges, answering different questions. **Management** (2% p.a. by default) is
 rent on parked capital: it accrues continuously with elapsed time and is charged
 whether the fund made money or not. **Performance** (20% by default) is a share of
 profit above the investor's OWN high-water mark, crystallized at the end of a
 period. A product with no policy charges nothing — the fee is opt-in per product.

 The mark is PER INVESTOR, not per fund. That is what stops one investor from paying
 for another's timing: somebody who subscribed at the top pays only on gains above
 the price they actually paid, and somebody who subscribed after a drawdown does not
 ride the recovery fee-free. (A fund-level mark, which a tokenized vault is forced
 into, mutualizes both.)

 A fee is collected by clawing back UNITS — the holder's fund units move to the
 product's fee class, held by the reserved `fee` allocation (#245: what the platform
 earns is that allocation's, and its holders are people) — never by moving cash. So: no chain
 fee is ever paid to collect a fee, an investor's cash balance is untouched and
 cannot be driven negative, and because total units outstanding do not change, NAV
 per unit does not move and no other investor pays for the charge. What cannot be
 collected (units locked by a queued redemption, or a residue below one base unit)
 is carried as debt and taken next time; it is never written off.

 SettleFeeShares is the one operation that crosses into cash, converting a whole
 fund's accumulated fee units in one go rather than once per investor — at the NAV of
 the day, out of the product's claim into the `fee` allocation's. Amounts and prices
 are exact decimal strings. See piggybank/core/PATTERNS.md and docs/FEES.md.

tags.name: banking.v1.HealthService
tags.description:
Health surface for the hub's gRPC service plane.

   Check     — liveness: is the process up? Trivial, unauthenticated; backs the
               `cabinet` BFF smoke path (browser -> BFF -> gRPC) and service checks.
   Readiness — can this instance actually move money? Pings Postgres + TigerBeetle
               and inspects the outbox (parked rows / dispatch backlog). An
               orchestrator/LB drains an instance that is up but not ready instead of
               routing money-moving traffic to it.

tags.name: banking.v1.WalletService
tags.description:
WalletService — a user's own crypto wallet: one unified USDT balance, deposit
 addresses, and withdrawals. Networks (BEP20/Polygon/TRC20/TON) are a transaction attribute
 (where you deposit / where a withdrawal ships), never a balance dimension — the user
 holds a single fungible USDT balance, segmented by lifecycle.

 Every RPC acts on the caller's own access-token `sub`. Balances are read live from the
 authoritative TigerBeetle ledger (Read-First); amounts are decimal USDT STRINGS
 (proto3 has no u128; a string is lossless and matches proto-loader's `longs: String`).
 A withdrawal is a queued saga (reserve → dispatch → settle/void): it is accepted even
 when the chosen rail is short on liquidity and queued until the treasury tops it up.
 The operator-driven dispatch/settle/fail RPCs live on BalanceService; the custody
 broadcast and deposit-address derivation sit behind ports (a stub in this scaffold).
 See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md and piggybank/core/PATTERNS.md.

tags.name: banking.v1.CompartmentService
tags.description:
CompartmentService — the caller's wallet split by scope (`main`, `invest`, `sa`, …),
 as on an exchange with sub-accounts: `main` is the wallet above (deposits arrive
 there, withdrawals leave from there); every other scope the user has entered holds
 a compartment, money earmarked for that scope's services. Only the user moves money
 between `main` and a compartment — instantly and without a fee — and never between
 two non-main scopes directly. A user is identified by their `auth_subject`.

 A separate service, not new fields on `Wallet`: WalletService keeps its shape while
 the compartments are built behind it, and its `Balance` carries only their sum
 (`in_compartments`). Every RPC acts on the caller's own `sub`.

 FIRST-PARTY ONLY. Every MUTATING wallet route — `WalletService.RequestWithdrawal`,
 `WalletService.CancelWithdrawal`, `MoveFunds`, `GrantMandate`, `RevokeMandate`, and
 `InvoicePaymentService.PayInvoice` — is accepted only from
 `Origin: https://evinvest.ltd`. A scope's host may read balances and history
 cross-origin; to act it opens the wallet page on evinvest.ltd and learns the result
 by `postMessage` with the origin checked. The CSRF token is never in a body a
 cross-origin read can see.

 FROZEN. A frozen user's new debits — MoveFunds into a scope, PayInvoice — are
 FAILED_PRECONDITION `user_frozen`; a FROZEN scope takes no MoveFunds in
 (`scope_frozen`), a CLOSED one neither (`scope_closed`). Credits, reads and MoveFunds
 back to `main` go on: that money never leaves the platform, so neither a freeze nor the
 outflow pause stops it.

tags.name: banking.v1.InvoicePaymentService
tags.description:
InvoicePaymentService — the payer's side of an invoice a scope issued
 (`scope.v1.InvoiceService`). The user opens it from the scope's link in the wallet
 page or the `<ev-pay-invoice>` element and pays it straight into the scope's
 account from `main` or from their compartment in that scope — no move between
 compartments first. Every RPC acts on the caller's own `sub`.

 Paying is first-party: `PayInvoice` is accepted only from
 `Origin: https://evinvest.ltd` (see `CompartmentService`), and an invoice's
 `pay_url` always points there. Whichever source pays, the RECEIVING scope's
 `min_kyc_level` applies to the payer (FAILED_PRECONDITION `kyc_level`); a frozen
 payer is `user_frozen`.

tags.name: banking.v1.OperationsService
tags.description:
OperationsService — the caller's activity timeline: every money event that touched
 their account, in one time-ordered stream.

 A pure CQRS **read model**. The four things a user does — deposit, withdraw,
 subscribe, redeem — are separate aggregates written through their own services
 (WalletService, FundsService); each already exposes its own list. What none of them
 can answer is "what happened, in order", because interleaving four lists client-side
 needs a timestamp every one of them must agree on. This service is that join, done
 once in the hub over the Postgres projections.

 Read-only: it moves no money and owns no state. Every RPC acts on the caller's own
 access-token `sub`. Amounts are decimal USDT STRINGS (proto3 has no u128; a string is
 lossless and matches proto-loader's `longs: String`).
 See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md and piggybank/core/PATTERNS.md.

tags.name: banking.v1.PaymentsService
tags.description:
PaymentsService — the ORDER that moves money between two named ends of the platform.

 Three tiers on one order, DERIVED from the destination and never supplied: an external
 wallet address (L1, settled by the withdrawal saga), a product's pooled claim
 `service:<id>` (L2, one posted transfer), any other internal claim (L3, one posted
 transfer). See domain/src/payments.rs for the aggregate and docs/CONSILIUM.md § Payments
 for the policy.

 AUTHORIZATION IS A FUNCTION OF THE SOURCE. A payment out of an allocation's pooled
 claim (`service:<id>` — a product's, or the platform's own `fee` / `fund`) needs the
 owners' consilium at every tier — the consilium is opened INSIDE OpenPayment, there is
 no separate RPC. A payment out of an investor's own claim (`user:<id>`) needs THAT
 investor's emailed consent at every tier. There is deliberately no cell in which one
 admin moves pooled money alone. The singleton `piggybank` / `revenue` sources are
 retired (#245) and a request naming them is refused. banking's treasury (`treasury`,
 D17) is the one source beside them that is not an allocation. It collects the withdrawal
 fees and is never a destination; as a source it is CLOSED until its spending is decided
 by concierge's scope approvals (`bank:treasury_surplus`, D24) — OpenPayment out of it is
 FAILED_PRECONDITION `treasury spending waits for scope approvals`.

 HOW THE APPROVAL IS SEATED. Two switches (`PAYMENT_APPROVALS_FUND`, default `consilium`;
 `PAYMENT_APPROVALS_SESSION`, default `concierge`) decide how a NEW order is seated. With
 `concierge`, the owners decide a fund-owned order over a concierge approval of kind
 `bank:payment` — proposed in the initiator's name, which needs their access token of the
 last two minutes in `x-ev-user-token` — and an investor's order is answered by that
 investor, signed in, over PaymentConfirmationService; no token and no mail are involved.
 With `consilium` new orders are seated on banking's consilium and the emailed token. An
 order keeps the seat it was opened with. See `Payment.seat`.

 IMMUTABILITY. There is no edit RPC. `payload_hash` binds the approval to the exact terms
 shown in the mail; changing anything means cancel and reopen.

tags.name: banking.v1.PaymentConsentService
tags.description:
PaymentConsentService — the surface an emailed investor reaches. Mounted OUTSIDE the
 user-auth layer, exactly as ConsiliumApprovalService is: the emailed token IS the
 credential, and the investor clicking it may not be signed in.

 The GET is strictly read-only because mail scanners issue automatic requests for every
 URL in a message. The consent is a separate call carrying the secret code from the same
 mail — that is what turns a scanned link into a deliberate human act.

tags.name: banking.v1.PaymentConfirmationService
tags.description:
PaymentConfirmationService — the investor's side of a payment out of THEIR claim, signed in.
 Behind the user-auth layer: the caller is the subject, and an order that is not theirs, has
 no such seat or does not exist is the same NOT_FOUND. It replaces the emailed token and
 code: the session is the credential, and the cabinet's gate asks for a fresh login before
 an approval (a decline asks for none).

tags.name: banking.v1.PayoutReviewService
tags.description:
PayoutReviewService — the lines of a `bank:scope_payout` operation, for the people who
 are asked to approve it (banking#529, SCOPE-LEDGER checklist item 9).

 The approval concierge shows carries only totals, the largest single line and two flags;
 the approvers could not see WHO is paid HOW MUCH. This is the read behind the page that
 shows them. It reads the operation banking STORED when the payout was requested — the same
 rows the approval's `lines_digest` was taken over and the executor pays from — never
 anything a caller sends.

 Read-only: it moves no money and writes nothing. Who may read is decided at the cabinet's
 BFF, which has the caller's concierge session: only a voter on the approval's frozen roster
 gets a page. This service refuses what it can check itself — an unknown operation, one that
 is not a payout, one whose approval is not opened, and a caller-supplied `approval_id` that
 is not the operation's own — all with one identical NOT_FOUND, so a probe learns nothing
 about which ids exist. Amounts are canonical decimal USDT strings.

tags.name: banking.v1.UsersService
tags.description:
UsersService — investor accounts and their investments.

 Identity metadata is the Postgres control plane; money is read live from the
 authoritative TigerBeetle ledger and is NEVER re-bookkept in Postgres. Every
 RPC is authorized from the verified access-token Claims injected by core's
 inbound auth layer; self-service RPCs act on the caller's own `sub`, admin RPCs
 are gated by the hub's admin allowlist (config). See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

tags.name: concierge.v1.UserDirectory
tags.description:
UserDirectory — the authoritative user/identity control plane.

 Owns investor accounts and their profile metadata. This is the identity plane:
 money lives in the separate banking plane and is NEVER mirrored here. Every RPC
 is authorized from the verified access-token Claims injected by the inbound auth
 layer; self-service RPCs act on the caller's own `sub`, admin RPCs are gated by
 the admin allowlist (config).

tags.name: concierge.v1.AuthService
tags.description:
AuthService — the concierge plane's token issuance and authorization surface.

 Issues first-party asymmetric JWTs (EdDSA/Ed25519), rotates refresh tokens, and
 publishes verification keys. Services do NOT call this per request to authorize:
 they verify access tokens locally against the cached JWKS via the shared
 `evconcierge_auth` flow (no round trip, no per-service token storage). They DO call
 `Jwks` periodically to refresh that cache, since concierge speaks only gRPC (no HTTP
 `.well-known` endpoint).

 Sign-in itself (Google, GitHub, emailed code, password) is the plane's own HTTP
 surface (`/auth/*`, reached as `evinvest.ltd/api/auth/*`), which opens the session
 in process; no RPC signs anybody in.

tags.name: concierge.v1.GovernanceService
tags.description:
GovernanceService — the fund's OWNERSHIP plane: who holds `Role::Owner`, and the
 consilium that must agree before a seat is taken away.

 WHY OWNERSHIP LIVES HERE. A seat is `users.role`, a concierge-owned fact, and the
 bridge to the money plane is one-way. Only this plane may mutate it, so only this
 plane can authorize the mutation. The money plane runs its own, separate consilium
 over its own mirrored roster — neither plane trusts the other's verdict.

 THE RULE. A removal passes when EITHER
   (a) the target accepts it from their own mailbox, OR
   (b) every owner except the target and the initiator votes to remove.

 Path (b) is unanimity over `owners \ {target, initiator}`. With exactly two owners
 that set is EMPTY and unanimity over it is vacuously true — which would let either
 owner expel the other unilaterally. Path (b) therefore requires at least ONE eligible
 peer voter; with two owners only path (a) exists.

 FLOOR. A removal may not leave fewer than TWO owners. Two suspends payouts — the
 money plane's `floor(N/2)+1` threshold is unreachable below three — but that is
 recoverable, because two owners can still admit a third. A floor of three was the
 earlier draft and it was wrong: at exactly three owners it made a bad actor
 unremovable forever, and a permanent deadlock is worse than a recoverable pause.

 ADMISSION IS GOVERNED TOO, and it is the reason the rest of this holds. Granting a
 seat is its own consilium: unanimity of `owners \ {initiator}`, with at least one such
 peer. Without it a bad actor mints sock puppets BEFORE opening an invoice and then
 reaches quorum legitimately — 2 honest owners plus 4 puppets is N=7, threshold 4,
 voters 6 — and snapshotting the roster cannot help, because the stuffing already
 happened. Unanimity rather than a majority, because a minority must never be able to
 grow itself into a majority.

 See banking's docs/CONSILIUM.md for the whole policy.

tags.name: concierge.v1.OwnerRemovalApprovalService
tags.description:
OwnerRemovalApprovalService — the surface the TARGET of a removal reaches from their
 mailbox. Mounted outside the user-auth layer, like AuthService: the emailed token is
 the credential, and the person clicking may not be signed in.

 The read is side-effect free because mail scanners issue automatic requests for every
 URL in a message; accepting requires the secret code from the same mail.

tags.name: concierge.v1.MailRelayService
tags.description:
MailRelayService — the one seam over which the MONEY plane asks this plane to send a
 governance mail, because this plane owns the only mailer (lettre + the delivery queue
 + backoff + the daily budget) and standing up a second one would duplicate all of it.

 Authenticated by the shared banking↔concierge service secret, compared in constant
 time, and mounted outside the user-auth layer exactly as the lifecycle bridge is.

 The payload is TYPED, never rendered HTML: this plane renders it. A compromised money
 plane must not be able to put arbitrary markup into an owner's mailbox.

 WHO MAY RECEIVE ONE is decided per KIND, and the default is the strict one. The
 consilium kinds — the three payout kinds and PAYMENT_APPROVAL — speak to the
 consilium, so they go to a seated owner and to nobody else — that rule is what stops a
 compromised money plane aiming a concierge-branded security mail at any address on
 the platform. PAYMENT_CONSENT cannot use it: consenting to a
 transfer of your own money has nothing to do with holding a seat. It gets its own rule,
 narrower in the dimension that matters — the recipient must BE the payment's subject,
 named in the typed payload — so the surface widens by exactly one person per message
 rather than to everyone. The fee policy pair follows the same split: FEE_POLICY_APPROVAL
 is a consilium kind (a seated owner, verified address), FEE_POLICY_NOTICE is addressed by
 identity to the one investor it is about.

 PAYMENT_OUTCOME — a payment that died while waiting for its subject's consent (the
 consent link burned on wrong codes, or was invalidated when the subject's sessions were
 revoked or their address changed) — speaks to two audiences at once, so it has the one
 two-armed rule: the recipient must BE the payment's subject, or hold a staff role
 (admin or owner) — the person who opened the order is usually an admin and holds no
 seat. It carries no link and no code: there is nothing left to decide.

 This path deliberately bypasses notification preferences. `NotificationService.Emit`
 is opt-out on both channels, and a security mail that a subscriber can silently
 switch off is not a security mail.
